claims.text: Advanced free-energy sampling–guided synthesis will enable formation of noble metal–based HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Free-energy sampling–guided synthesis will provide precise atomic control and overcome limitations of conventional NM-HEA synthesis.
The proposed starting materials are bulk NM-HEA precursors with high configurational entropy.
The bulk NM-HEA precursors lack a defined three-dimensional nanostructure.
NM-HEA precursors exhibit phase separation under conventional synthesis conditions.
Advanced free-energy methods such as umbrella sampling or metadynamics can be applied during NM-HEA synthesis.
Temperature, pressure, and chemical potential can be controlled in conjunction with free-energy sampling to direct NM-HEA synthesis.
Free-energy landscapes can be mapped in situ during synthesis to direct atomic assembly.
The intervention will produce a three-dimensional interconnected NM-HEA nanoframework.
Each atomic species will be uniformly incorporated into the nanoframework.
Mapping the free-energy landscape modulates the nucleation barrier and growth pathways of NM-HEAs.
Modulation of nucleation and growth pathways enables atomic-level control during framework formation.
The free-energy sampling approach prevents phase separation and coalescence during framework formation.
The resulting NM-HEA catalysts will have a well-defined three-dimensional nanoframework and uniform atomic distribution.
The resulting nanoframework catalysts will exhibit improved catalytic performance relative to conventionally synthesized materials.
Traditional NM-HEA synthesis typically produces less-controlled nanostructures with phase separation and coalescence.
Phase separation, coalescence, and poor nanostructural control lead to inferior catalytic properties.
Without free-energy sampling or precise control of temperature, pressure, and chemical potential, the NM-HEA will lack a defined three-dimensional framework.
High-resolution TEM, XRD, and surface spectroscopy can assess framework morphology, phase behavior, and atomic distribution.
